node.label: Frances A. Yates
node.date_label: Renaissance culture and arts of memory · 1960s–70s
node.description: Investigates mnemonic techniques, images and Renaissance intellectual culture through textual and visual reconstruction. The Art of Memory distinguishes traditions of remembering and argues that their transformations matter to the history of knowledge. Named collaborators and critics help expose both the resources and risks of this inquiry.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Art of Memory (1966), including its treatment of Renaissance memory systems and questions about scientific method. Her historical interpretations are arguments for assessment, not a single uncontested model of Renaissance thought. Further selected bibliography: Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition (1964).
node.scope_note: The complete preface and concluding chapter distinguish classical rhetoric, medieval prudence, Lullism and Renaissance occult memory. Yates uses Rossi without claiming identical approaches; Bing mediates Warburg’s image questions, and Walker and R. W. Yates contribute specific work. Leibniz and secret-transmission arguments retain their hypothetical or contested status. Mnemonic arts differ from collective commemoration; Yates is not assigned a Skinner-derived method or Cambridge School membership. Canonical-work review (2026-10-24): added titles and dates are selected bibliography, not a complete career or a new reading of the books. Original works, translations, edited collections and posthumous editions are distinguished; earlier argument and source-reading qualifications remain.

incident_edges.relationship: invites comparison of Renaissance cultural forms and historical meanings
incident_edges.evidence_note: Affinity in subjects is not proof of direct descent from Burckhardt or Huizinga. The primary preface now documents a distinct Warburg setting and collaborators; no Burckhardt/Huizinga transmission is established.

incident_edges.relationship: investigates connections between memory systems and histories of knowledge
incident_edges.evidence_note: The Art of Memory’s contents include scientific-method questions; this does not equate Yates’s approach with Kuhn, SSK, or STS. Complete chapter XVII pp. 368–389 now supports an attributed argument about mnemonic ordering, combinatory projects and methods. Stronger causal and secret-transmission hypotheses remain unverified.

incident_edges.relationship: contrasts mnemonic arts with collective memory and commemoration
incident_edges.evidence_note: A teaching distinction, not a claim that Yates founded or directly produced the later memory-studies field. The primary preface differentiates several techniques and their intellectual/religious uses; that scope does not establish a direct genealogy of collective-memory scholarship.

incident_edges.relationship: compares Renaissance intellectual inquiry with contextual histories of argument
incident_edges.evidence_note: Different approaches to historical meanings; Yates is not assigned Cambridge School membership or a Skinner-derived method. The primary preface places Bruno historically while using distinct textual/visual resources. Shared contextual concern is an editorial comparison, not membership evidence.

incident_edges.relationship: Hill names Yates’s work as a resource for reconstructing earlier intellectual settings
incident_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 1–6 relates magic, religion and rationality historically. This acknowledged resource does not establish that Hill accepted every Yates thesis.

incident_edges.relationship: Bing, Gombrich, Walker and R. W. Yates contribute to Yates’s reconstruction
incident_edges.evidence_note: Primary preface names draft criticism, discussions, translation checking and drawings. Warburg’s questions reach Yates through Bing, not personal contact. The proposed Globe reconstruction is an argument, not a verified building plan.

incident_edges.relationship: Rossi’s memory research supplies a resource Yates uses with qualifications
incident_edges.evidence_note: Preface xiii and chapter XVII explicitly use Clavis universalis (1960); pp. 372–373 qualify agreement over Bacon. Rossi’s full book is not independently read.
incident_edges.map_label: Rossi: a resource with different emphases

incident_edges.relationship: Gombrich recalls evidential hesitation and internal criticism alongside admiration
incident_edges.evidence_note: The complete 1983 memorial describes Bing/Saxl criticism and Yates’s defense of larger interpretations. It declines full evaluation; no case-by-case disproof or unanimous Warburg position is claimed.

incident_edges.relationship: Le Goff draws on Yates’s account of artificial memory and its Renaissance transformations, including her interpretations of memory theatres and Bruno.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Sustained attributed use and explicit praise, printed 458–460. Yates’s reconstructions remain her interpretations as used by Le Goff; neither their universal acceptance nor her entire hermetic account is asserted. The cited 1966 book is not newly read.

verification.note: Publisher sample title/copyright, dedication, complete preface ix–x and introduction 1–6 read. Radical alternatives, porous labels, publication conditions and changing questions are explicit. Names Hilton as draft reader, Morton/Nuttall/Thomas as resources, and Yates/Rattansi/Webster in reconstructing intellectual settings. Chapters 2 onward and original notes not read; 2019 sample preserves 1972 original and later Penguin note. Previous scope: Publisher sample title and copyright pages checked: 1972 original, 2019 edition. This does not independently verify every classification of Hill’s work.

verification.note: Publisher description and contents, plus primary introduction opening at DOI 10.1017/CBO9780511572999.002, consulted. Description proposes distinct assumptions/methods and questions a simple magic-to-science transition; opening criticizes older dismissals of occult inquiry. Full introduction and cases unread. No direct Vickers-to-Yates critique arrow is inferred from the opening alone; the proposed distinction remains debatable.
